title: AFDRS Fire Danger Rating Operational Actions
summary: Derived note from the Australian Fire Danger Rating System and NSW RFS public guidance: use fire danger ratings as action triggers, not as incident warnings.
content: The Australian Fire Danger Rating System provides national public fire danger categories that indicate the possible consequences if a fire starts. Moderate means plan and prepare. High means be ready to act. Extreme means take action now to protect life and property. Catastrophic means leaving bushfire risk areas is the survival-oriented action. Operational dashboards must not treat a fire danger rating as proof that a fire is occurring; it is a preparedness and consequence indicator. When a hotspot cluster is active and the rating is High, Extreme, or Catastrophic, escalate monitoring, check warnings, review exposed assets, and prepare internal briefings. Public-facing language should point users to official fire agency ratings and warnings.
source_title: NSW RFS Fire Danger Ratings; Australian Fire Danger Rating System

title: NSW RFS Bush Fire Alert Levels Interpretation
summary: Derived note from NSW RFS alert-level guidance: Advice, Watch and Act, and Emergency Warning are threat-level messages for active fires.
content: NSW RFS explains that bush fire alert levels indicate the level of threat from a fire. Advice means a fire has started and there is no immediate danger, but people should stay up to date. Watch and Act means conditions are changing and people need to start taking action to protect themselves and family. Emergency Warning is the highest level and means people may be in danger and need to take action immediately. Operational reports must distinguish these warning levels from dashboard risk scores. If no official warning feed is available or no warning is found, say official warning coverage is unavailable or no matching warning was found; do not imply an area is safe.
source_title: NSW RFS Alert Levels

title: DFES WA Bushfire Decision Guidance
summary: Derived note from DFES WA bushfire pages: bushfires are unpredictable, conditions can change quickly, and indecision is a major public safety risk.
content: DFES WA public guidance emphasizes that bushfires are unpredictable, can change quickly, and require people to make decisions early. Operational AI should therefore avoid soft language when evidence shows active hotspots, deteriorating weather, exposed assets, or an official warning. For Western Australia AOIs, cite Emergency WA or DFES as the authoritative public warning source. Internal recommendations can prioritize monitoring, field intelligence, access-route review, and draft communications, but public instructions such as evacuation, shelter, road closure, or all-clear must come from official warning products.
source_title: DFES WA Bushfire Overview and During a Bushfire

title: AIDR Evacuation Planning Principles
summary: Derived note from the Australian Disaster Resilience Handbook: evacuation planning should use an all-hazards approach and adapt to time, place, and circumstance.
content: AIDR evacuation planning guidance uses an all-hazards planning approach and recognizes nationally used evacuation stages. For this agent, evacuation-related outputs must be treated as high-risk operational content. The agent may flag that evacuation planning considerations could be relevant when official warnings, access constraints, exposed settlements, or fast-changing fire behaviour are present. It must not issue evacuation orders. If evacuation language is requested, produce a draft for human review and cite the need for official agency confirmation, local context, transport/access assessment, vulnerable people considerations, and traffic management coordination.
source_title: AIDR Evacuation Planning Handbook

title: Official Warning and Public Communications Boundary
summary: Internal control: dashboard risk alerts are not official warnings; public communications must preserve the distinction.
content: Wildfire Ops risk scores, hotspot density, weather pressure, and spatial exposure are analytical decision-support outputs. They are not official public warnings. Public communications generated by the agent must remain drafts until a human approves them. The draft must avoid official command language such as evacuate now, shelter now, road closed, all clear, or fire contained unless that wording is copied from or explicitly supported by an official emergency agency warning. If warning coverage is pending or unavailable for a state, say coverage is unavailable rather than saying there is no warning.
source_title: NSW RFS Alert Levels; DFES Emergency WA Prepare

title: Inspection Prioritization: Exposure, Weather, and Access
summary: Operational playbook derived from fire danger, warning, and evacuation-planning guidance: rank hotspot clusters by exposure, weather pressure, warning status, and access constraints.
content: When multiple hotspot clusters are active, do not rank only by hotspot count. Prioritize clusters where recent detections overlap or sit near populated places, critical infrastructure, road corridors, protected areas, or other values at risk. Increase priority when the latest weather evidence shows stronger wind gusts, low humidity, limited recent rainfall, or a forecast deterioration. Increase priority when official warnings are present or when warning coverage is unavailable but the evidence indicates fast-changing conditions. Before recommending field inspection, note access and crew-safety uncertainty. If access-route or road-closure data is not available, say so explicitly.
source_title: NSW RFS Fire Danger Ratings; AIDR Evacuation Planning Handbook

title: Weather Escalation Signals: Wind, Humidity, and Rainfall
summary: Operational note: wind, low humidity, and dry antecedent conditions should be interpreted as escalation signals, not standalone warnings.
content: Fire danger ratings are driven by forecast weather and fuel conditions. For dashboard analysis, rising wind gusts, low relative humidity, and limited recent rainfall should increase concern, especially when active hotspots are present. If the user asks what changed since yesterday, compare matched run baselines or matched weather observations only. If no yesterday baseline exists, say the change cannot be calculated and provide current wind, humidity, and rainfall evidence. Do not infer a wind change from a single current forecast.
source_title: NSW RFS Fire Danger Ratings

title: WA Emergency Information Source Hierarchy
summary: Derived note from Emergency WA and DFES: use Emergency WA, ABC/local news, and DFES recorded information as public information channels.
content: Emergency WA directs the public to check warnings and incidents, listen to local ABC radio or news bulletins, follow emergency services updates, and call 000 in a life-threatening emergency. For WA outputs, the agent should treat Emergency WA/DFES as the source of public warning status. Internal analysis may cite hotspot, weather, and spatial evidence, but public advice should direct users to official warning channels and emergency numbers. If a user asks for public advice, draft concise text and keep it pending approval.
source_title: Emergency WA Prepare

title: Data Source Reliability and Limitations
summary: Operational note: distinguish live observations/forecasts, official warnings, spatial exposure, and derived Elastic policy memory.
content: DEA hotspots, weather forecasts, official warning feeds, spatial exposure APIs, and Elastic policy memory have different reliability roles. Hotspots show detections, not confirmed incident status. Weather forecasts show forecast pressure, not observed fire behaviour. Spatial exposure identifies nearby assets and protected areas when provider coverage is available, but may not include road closures, live traffic, settlement exposure, or crew-safety constraints. Elastic MCP stores searchable operational memory derived from official guidance and internal controls; it is not a live warning source. Reports should state which sources were used and which categories were missing or unavailable.
source_title: Emergency WA Prepare; NSW RFS Alert Levels; AIDR Evacuation Planning Handbook

title: Human Approval for External Actions
summary: Internal control: the agent may draft advisories, emails, and field-team briefs, but must not execute external actions.
content: Because official public warnings and emergency instructions are issued by responsible agencies, the agent must not independently publish public advisories, send emergency-service emails, direct field crews, declare road closures, or issue evacuation/shelter instructions. It may draft internal briefs, public advisory drafts, and rationale for review. Drafts should include the monitored region, evidence sources, uncertainty, official warning status, and a clear note that final release requires human approval and official-source verification.
source_title: NSW RFS Alert Levels; AIDR Evacuation Planning Handbook

title: Public Advisory Drafting Policy
summary: Supersedes the earlier generic policy: public advisory text must follow official warning principles and stay in draft until approved.
content: The agent may draft public advisory language, but must not publish or represent it as an official warning. AIDR public information and warning guidance treats effective warnings as timely, targeted, tailored communication that supports protective action. Drafts should identify the hazard, affected area, current evidence, official warning status, uncertainty, and the source that operators must verify before release. If no official warning feed is available, say warning coverage is unavailable. Do not downgrade risk to safe because a warning was not retrieved. Use Australian Warning System wording only when the relevant official agency warning supports it.
source_title: AIDR Public Information and Warnings Handbook; Australian Warning System

title: External Action Boundary Policy
summary: Supersedes the earlier generic boundary: the agent can recommend monitoring and drafts, but cannot issue emergency instructions or direct field actions.
content: External emergency actions remain the responsibility of accountable agencies and human operators. The agent must not issue evacuation orders, shelter instructions, road closures, all-clear statements, field crew deployment orders, or public warnings. It can prepare internal briefs, monitoring tasks, inspection priorities, and draft communications for review. When a user requests an external action, the output should separate evidence, rationale, and proposed draft text, then require official-source verification and human approval before release or execution.
source_title: AIDR Public Information and Warnings Handbook; AIDR Incident Management Handbook

title: Wildfire Operations Risk Playbook
summary: Supersedes the earlier generic playbook: combine fire danger, hotspot activity, weather pressure, official warnings, exposure, and access uncertainty.
content: Operational prioritization should combine several evidence streams rather than using hotspot count alone. Use fire danger ratings as preparedness and consequence triggers, active hotspots as detection evidence, weather as escalation pressure, official warnings as public threat status, and spatial exposure as values-at-risk context. Rank first the AOI where active hotspots overlap with stronger wind, low humidity, dry conditions, exposed settlements, roads, critical infrastructure, protected areas, or unavailable access information. Treat HIGH or worse risk as a reason to increase monitoring cadence and prepare human-reviewed operational briefs. Do not present derived risk scores as official warnings.
source_title: NSW RFS Fire Danger Ratings; WA State Hazard Plan Fire; AIDR Incident Management Handbook

title: Official Warning Interpretation Guide
summary: Supersedes the earlier generic guide: interpret Advice, Watch and Act, and Emergency Warning as official warning levels, not internal risk labels.
content: The Australian Warning System uses three levels: Advice, Watch and Act, and Emergency Warning. Advice indicates an incident has started with no immediate danger and people should stay up to date. Watch and Act indicates heightened threat and changing conditions requiring action. Emergency Warning is the highest warning level and indicates immediate action may be needed. Internal risk labels such as MODERATE or HIGH are not warning levels. If the system has no matching official warning, say no matching warning was retrieved or coverage is unavailable; do not infer there is no danger.
source_title: Australian Warning System; NSW RFS Alert Levels

title: Fire Weather Scenario Thresholds
summary: Supersedes the earlier generic threshold: weather signals should be interpreted with fire danger ratings and active fire evidence.
content: Wind, humidity, temperature, rainfall deficit, and fire danger ratings should be treated as scenario drivers rather than standalone proof of incident severity. Increase concern when current or forecast conditions show stronger gusts, low relative humidity, limited rainfall, or a High, Extreme, or Catastrophic fire danger rating near active hotspots. If the user asks whether conditions changed since yesterday, compare a matched baseline from previous runs or weather observations. If the baseline is missing, report current conditions and explicitly state that the change cannot be calculated.
source_title: NSW RFS Fire Danger Ratings; Australian Fire Danger Rating System

title: Inspection Prioritization SOP
summary: Supersedes the earlier generic SOP: prioritize inspection candidates by evidence, exposure, access uncertainty, and incident-management consequences.
content: When asked which area to inspect first, answer the specific prioritization question. Rank AOIs by active hotspot concentration, recency, weather pressure, official warning status, critical assets, towns, roads, protected areas, and access uncertainty. If protected areas or critical assets are present, include them in the monitoring watchlist. If access-route data, road closures, or crew-safety information are missing, state that limitation before recommending field inspection. Recommendations are internal priorities for operator review, not deployment orders.
source_title: AIDR Incident Management Handbook; AIDR Emergency Planning Handbook

title: Wind and Low Humidity Escalation Scenario
summary: Supersedes the earlier unsourced historical pattern: use this as a scenario pattern, not as a claimed historical incident.
content: A scenario with active hotspots, strengthening winds, low humidity, and limited recent rainfall should be treated as an escalation pattern. The agent should monitor wind direction and gust changes, humidity minima, hotspot movement, new detections, official warning changes, and exposure to people, roads, assets, and protected areas. Do not call the pattern a historical incident unless a specific source document is attached. If the evidence is only current forecast and current hotspots, describe it as an operational scenario.
source_title: NSW RFS Fire Danger Ratings; AIDR Incident Management Handbook

title: Data Source Reliability Notes
summary: Supersedes the earlier generic note: define the role and limits of hotspots, weather, warnings, spatial exposure, and Elastic policy memory.
content: Hotspots are detection evidence, not confirmation of incident control status. Weather forecasts are pressure indicators, not direct observations of fire behaviour. Official warnings are authoritative public threat products when available. Spatial exposure APIs can identify nearby assets, roads, towns, or protected areas, but may miss local access constraints and live closures. Elastic MCP evidence is policy and protocol memory derived from official guidance and internal controls; it is not a live operational feed. Reports should cite what evidence was used and say what evidence was unavailable.
source_title: AIDR Public Information and Warnings Handbook; AIDR Incident Management Handbook; Emergency WA Prepare

title: Australian Warning System Protocol
summary: Protocol for mapping official warning levels and calls to action without confusing them with internal risk scores.
content: Use Australian Warning System levels only for official warning products: Advice, Watch and Act, and Emergency Warning. Calls to action such as Stay informed, Monitor conditions, Prepare to leave, Leave now, Prepare to take shelter, Move indoors, Avoid the area, or Not safe to return must be treated as official-warning language unless clearly marked as a draft for review. The agent may quote or summarize official warning language when sourced, but should otherwise use internal recommendation wording such as monitor, verify, prepare briefing, review exposure, or escalate for human assessment.
source_title: Australian Warning System

title: Public Information and Warnings Protocol
summary: Protocol for emergency communications: make information timely, targeted, tailored, sourced, and approval-gated.
content: Emergency communication should be timely, targeted, and tailored to the affected community and hazard. The agent should separate public information from official warnings, identify the evidence base, and avoid unsupported certainty. For generated advisories, include a title, affected AOI, current evidence, official warning status, recommended verification source, uncertainty, and approval status. If the user asks for a public message, produce a draft and state that it requires human approval and official agency verification before publication.
source_title: AIDR Public Information and Warnings Handbook

title: Incident Management Protocol
summary: Protocol for incident-management outputs: prepare, respond, transition to recovery, and reduce escalation risk.
content: Incident management covers preparation for effective response, response to the incident, and transition to recovery. For Wildfire Ops, the agent should produce decision-support outputs that reduce the likelihood of escalation: situation summary, changed conditions, exposed values, uncertainty, monitoring tasks, and recommended next checks. It should not claim command authority. When consequences could include injury, environmental damage, infrastructure disruption, or loss of public trust, prioritize clear limitations and escalation to human operators.
source_title: AIDR Incident Management Handbook

title: Emergency Planning Protocol
summary: Protocol for planning-oriented answers: use all-hazards planning principles, plan for uncertainty, and separate preparedness from live commands.
content: Emergency planning should support prevention, preparedness, response, and recovery, and should account for uncertainty. For the agent, planning outputs should identify assumptions, missing evidence, roles requiring human confirmation, monitoring cadence, decision triggers, and review points. Planning recommendations can include preparing internal briefs, checking official warnings, reviewing vulnerable assets, and validating access routes. They must not be framed as live emergency orders unless sourced from an official warning.
source_title: AIDR Emergency Planning Handbook

title: WA State Hazard Plan Fire Protocol
summary: Protocol derived from WA State Hazard Plan Fire: treat fire management as prevention, preparedness, response, and recovery under DFES/SEMC arrangements.
content: For Western Australia AOIs, treat DFES and Emergency WA as authoritative public information and warning channels. WA State Hazard Plan Fire describes arrangements for managing fire across prevention, preparedness, response, and recovery, with the FES Commissioner as Hazard Management Agency for fire and DFES maintaining the plan under SEMC delegation. The agent should align WA outputs to those arrangements: cite Emergency WA/DFES for public warning status, keep operational recommendations internal, and escalate uncertainty around access, exposed communities, protected areas, and official warning coverage.
source_title: WA State Hazard Plan Fire
